---
title: "Lazy API & Query Optimization"
subtitle: "≈ dbplyr · `arrow::open_dataset()` · duckplyr"
jupyter: python3
---

A `LazyFrame` is a query that has not run yet. Polars rewrites it before it
runs, so a lazy pipeline can skip files, columns and rows that an eager one
must read first and throw away later. This chapter covers how to read the
plan, each rewrite the optimizer makes (shown in a plan), what the default
streaming engine changes, a timed eager-vs-lazy comparison, and the traps.
The basics (`scan_*`, `collect()`, `explain()`) are in the
[Overview](../overview/polars-overview.qmd#sec-ov-lazy) and the
[cheatsheet](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-lazy).

## In tidyverse {#sec-lazy-tidyverse}

```r
library(dplyr)

# dbplyr: verbs build SQL; the database plans and runs it
jfk_late <- tbl(con, "flights") |>
  filter(origin == "JFK", dep_delay > 60) |>
  group_by(carrier) |>
  summarise(n = n(), avg_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))
show_query(jfk_late)   # the SQL
explain(jfk_late)      # the SQL plus the database's query plan
collect(jfk_late)      # run it, return a tibble

# arrow: verbs build an Acero plan over a directory of Parquet files
arrow::open_dataset("flights/") |>        # discovers files and schema, reads no rows
  filter(origin == "JFK") |>
  select(carrier, dep_delay) |>
  collect()

# duckplyr: the same verbs, planned and run by DuckDB
duckplyr::read_parquet_duckdb("flights.parquet") |> filter(origin == "JFK") |> explain()
```

All three split *describe* from *run*: verbs grow a query object, a backend
plans it, and `collect()` executes it. Polars is all three roles in one
library: the `LazyFrame` is the query object, and Polars' own optimizer and
engines plan and run it. There is no translation to SQL, so every expression
that works eagerly also works lazily.

|  | dbplyr | arrow `open_dataset()` | duckplyr | Polars |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| The plan is written in | SQL | an Acero exec plan | a DuckDB relational plan | a Polars logical plan |
| Show the plan | `show_query()`, `explain()` | `show_exec_plan()` | `explain()` | `lf.explain()` |
| Run, return a data frame | `collect()` | `collect()` | `collect()` | `lf.collect()` |
| Run, keep the result out of R | `compute()` (a database table) | `write_dataset()` | `compute_parquet()` | `lf.sink_parquet()` |

: One pattern, four backends {.striped}

## Mental model {#sec-lazy-model}

```text
 BUILD (plain Python, no data)     OPTIMIZE (at explain / collect)          EXECUTE (collect / sink)
 ─────────────────────────────     ──────────────────────────────────       ─────────────────────────────────
 pl.scan_parquet(path)             naive plan ──► optimized plan            streaming engine (default):
   .filter(...)            ─────►   • filters move into the scan   ─────►    batches flow through all
   .group_by(...)                   • the scan reads only used columns        operators at once
   .agg(...)                        • head()/slice move into the scan       in-memory engine:
                                    • duplicate expressions/subplans          each node finishes its whole
 a LazyFrame = a tree of plan         run once                                result before the next starts
 nodes; print(lf) shows the         • sorts nobody observes are dropped     ──► DataFrame (collect)
 naive plan                        lf.explain() prints this                 ──► files     (sink_*)
```

Two consequences drive everything below:

- **The optimizer sees the whole query.** An eager `read_parquet()` can't
  know that you will keep 3 of 19 columns and a few percent of the rows. A
  scan that is still in the plan can.
- **Nothing is checked or computed until something asks.** `collect()`,
  `collect_schema()` and `explain()` ask; building the plan does not.

## Mechanics {#sec-lazy-mechanics}

```{python}
#| include: false
%xmode Minimal
```

Every file in this chapter goes into a temporary directory that is deleted at
the end. `show_plan()` prints `lf.explain()` with that directory shortened
to `<tmp>` and random cache ids masked, so the plans read the same on every
render.

```{python}
import re
import tempfile
import time
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
from polars.testing import assert_frame_equal
from pl_notes import datasets

tmp = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
data_dir = Path(tmp.name)

flights_df = datasets.flights()
airlines_df = datasets.airlines()
flights_df.write_parquet(data_dir / "flights.parquet")
airlines_df.write_parquet(data_dir / "airlines.parquet")


def show_plan(plan: pl.LazyFrame | str, **kwargs) -> None:
    """print(plan.explain(**kwargs)), with the temp path and random ids masked."""
    text = plan if isinstance(plan, str) else plan.explain(**kwargs)
    text = text.replace(str(data_dir), "<tmp>")
    print(re.sub(r"[0-9a-f]{8}(-[0-9a-f]{4}){3}-[0-9a-f]{12}", "<id>", text))
```

### Sources: scan, don't read {#sec-lazy-sources}

```{python}
flights_lf = pl.scan_parquet(data_dir / "flights.parquet")
airlines_lf = pl.scan_parquet(data_dir / "airlines.parquet")

show_plan(flights_lf)
```

A one-node plan: a scan that would read all 19 columns. Displaying
`flights_lf` in a notebook shows the same naive plan, never rows.

| Source | Function | What the reader can skip |
|---|---|---|
| Parquet file, directory, or glob | `pl.scan_parquet()` | columns, rows (filters, row-group statistics, hive partitions), slices |
| CSV | `pl.scan_csv()` | columns, rows (filters applied while parsing), slices |
| NDJSON | `pl.scan_ndjson()` | columns, rows |
| Arrow IPC / Feather | `pl.scan_ipc()` | columns, rows |
| an in-memory `DataFrame` | `df.lazy()` | columns only: the data is already in memory |

: Lazy sources {.striped}

### Reading a plan {#sec-lazy-explain}

```{python}
jfk_late_lf = (
    flights_lf
    .filter(pl.col("origin") == "JFK", pl.col("dep_delay") > 60)
    .group_by("carrier")
    .agg(n=pl.len(), avg_delay=pl.col("dep_delay").mean())
    .sort("n", descending=True)
)
show_plan(jfk_late_lf, optimized=False)
```

That is the plan as written. `explain()` prints the tree root first, so
**read it bottom-up**: data enters at the scan (19 columns), passes the two
filters, is aggregated, then sorted. Each `FROM` points at the child node.
Now the plan that will actually run:

```{python}
show_plan(jfk_late_lf)
```

Two rewrites happened. **Predicate pushdown**: both filters disappeared into
the scan as one `SELECTION`, so the reader drops rows as it reads them.
**Projection pushdown**: the scan reads 3 of 19 columns, `origin` only so it
can filter, and just `carrier` and `dep_delay` go on to the aggregation
(`simple π`; π is relational-algebra notation for projection). Parquet
stores each column separately, so the other 16 are never touched on disk.

| Node | Meaning | dplyr / SQL analogue |
|---|---|---|
| `Parquet SCAN`, `Csv SCAN`, `DF [...]` | a source; `DF` is an in-memory frame | `FROM` |
| `PROJECT k/n COLUMNS` (in a scan) | columns the reader reads | `SELECT a, b` pushed into the reader |
| `SELECTION:` (in a scan) | a filter applied by the reader | `WHERE` pushed into the reader |
| `SLICE:` (in a scan) | rows the reader stops after | `LIMIT` |
| `ESTIMATED ROWS:` | size estimate used for join planning | |
| `FILTER … FROM` | a filter that stays where it was written | `filter()` |
| `simple π k/n [...]` | picks columns, computes nothing | `select(a, b)` |
| `SELECT [...]`, `WITH_COLUMNS:` | evaluates expressions | `transmute()`, `mutate()` |
| `AGGREGATE … BY … FROM` | group-by aggregation | `summarise(.by = )` |
| `SORT BY` (`[slice: …]` = top-k) | sort | `arrange()`, `slice_max()` |
| `… JOIN: LEFT PLAN … RIGHT PLAN` | a join, both inputs indented | `inner_join()` |
| `CACHE[id: …]` | a subplan computed once and read again | `compute()` |
| `OPAQUE_PYTHON` | a Python function the optimizer can't see into | |

: Plan nodes you will meet {.striped}

`explain(format="tree")` draws the same plan as a box diagram, and
`lf.show_graph()` renders it with Graphviz.

### The optimizations, one plan each {#sec-lazy-optimizations}

Each optimization rewrites the tree, and each has a flag in
`pl.QueryOptFlags` that turns it off. Turning one off is the easiest way to
see what it did.

#### Predicate pushdown {#sec-lazy-predicate}

A filter written *after* a join:

```{python}
show_plan(
    flights_lf.join(airlines_lf, on="carrier")
    .filter(pl.col("origin") == "JFK", pl.col("carrier") == "AA")
    .select("name", "dep_delay")
)
```

Each condition moved to the earliest point that has its columns:
`origin == "JFK"` into the flights scan, and `carrier == "AA"` into **both**
scans, because `carrier` is the join key. Projection pushdown needs no
separate demo: every optimized plan here shows it as `PROJECT k/n COLUMNS`.

#### Slice pushdown {#sec-lazy-slice}

```{python}
show_plan(flights_lf.head(5))
print("---")
show_plan(flights_lf.sort("dep_delay", descending=True).head(3))
```

`head(5)` became a `SLICE` inside the reader: preview a huge file and only
the first rows are read. `sort().head(3)` became a top-k sort
(`SORT BY [slice: (0, 3, …)]`), and the scan received a *dynamic predicate*:
a filter whose threshold the top-k node raises as it finds larger values, so
rows that can no longer make the top 3 are dropped as they are read. This is
dplyr's `slice_max(dep_delay, n = 3)`, derived automatically from
`sort` + `head`.

#### Expression simplification {#sec-lazy-simplify}

```{python}
not_late_lf = flights_lf.filter(~(pl.col("dep_delay") > 10)).select("dep_delay")
show_plan(not_late_lf)
print("---")
show_plan(not_late_lf, optimizations=pl.QueryOptFlags(simplify_expression=False))
```

`~(dep_delay > 10)` became `dep_delay <= 10`: one comparison instead of a
comparison plus a negation.

#### Common subexpressions and subplans {#sec-lazy-cse}

[Expressions & Contexts](../core/expressions.qmd#sec-expr-parallel) shows
an expression reused through a Python variable being computed once
(`__POLARS_CSER_…`). With that rewrite off, it is computed twice:

```{python}
delay_hr = pl.col("dep_delay") / 60
show_plan(
    flights_lf.select(delay_hr=delay_hr, delay_hr_sq=delay_hr**2),
    optimizations=pl.QueryOptFlags(comm_subexpr_elim=False),
)
```

The same idea at the level of whole plans: a lazy frame used twice, here as
both sides of a join.

```{python}
jfk_flights_lf = flights_lf.filter(pl.col("origin") == "JFK")

carrier_stats_lf = jfk_flights_lf.group_by("carrier").agg(n=pl.len()).join(
    jfk_flights_lf.group_by("carrier").agg(avg_delay=pl.col("dep_delay").mean()),
    on="carrier",
)
show_plan(carrier_stats_lf)
```

The right side reads `CACHE[id: <id>]` with nothing under it: it reuses the
left side's scan instead of reading the file again. In dbplyr you would get
this only by calling `compute()` yourself.

#### Sorts nobody observes {#sec-lazy-sorts}

```{python}
show_plan(flights_lf.sort("dep_delay").group_by("carrier").agg(pl.len()))
print("---")
show_plan(
    flights_lf.sort("dep_delay")
    .sort("arr_delay", maintain_order=True)
    .select("dep_delay", "arr_delay")
)
```

In the first plan the sort is gone: an unordered `group_by` can't observe
it. In the second, two sorts became one sort with two keys. R's sorting is
stable, so `arrange(dep_delay) |> arrange(arr_delay)` breaks ties in
`arr_delay` by `dep_delay`. Polars' `sort()` is not stable unless you pass
`maintain_order=True`; without it, the first sort is dropped entirely.

#### All the flags

| `pl.QueryOptFlags(...)` | What it does | Shown in |
|---|---|---|
| `predicate_pushdown` | moves filters toward (and into) the scan | @sec-lazy-predicate |
| `projection_pushdown` | reads only columns used later | every plan |
| `slice_pushdown` | moves `head`/`slice` toward the scan | @sec-lazy-slice |
| `simplify_expression` | rewrites expressions into simpler equivalents | @sec-lazy-simplify |
| `comm_subexpr_elim` | computes duplicate expressions once | @sec-lazy-cse |
| `comm_subplan_elim` | computes duplicate subplans once (`CACHE`) | @sec-lazy-cse |
| `check_order_observe` | drops ordering work whose order is never observed | @sec-lazy-sorts |
| `sort_collapse` | merges consecutive sorts into one | @sec-lazy-sorts |
| `cluster_with_columns` | merges sequential independent `with_columns` | |
| `fast_projection` | runs column-only projections without the expression engine (`simple π`) | |
| `join_order` | reorders chains of inner equi-joins by estimated size | |
| `row_estimate` | uses row estimates to pick join build sides | |
| `pre_partition_hive` | pre-partitions hive-partitioned joins on the partition key | |

: All default to `True`; `pl.QueryOptFlags.none()` starts with all off {.striped}

`collect()`, `sink_*()` and `pl.collect_all()` take the same
`optimizations=` argument. The API is marked **unstable**. In Polars 1.x the
flags were keyword arguments of `collect()`; 2.0 removed them (@sec-lazy-gotchas).
The naive plan in @sec-lazy-explain is what `pl.QueryOptFlags.none()` gives.

### Execution: the streaming engine {#sec-lazy-execution}

| `collect(engine=…)` | What runs |
|---|---|
| `"auto"` (default) | the engine set by `pl.Config.set_engine_affinity()` or `POLARS_ENGINE_AFFINITY`; if neither is set, **streaming** |
| `"streaming"` | the source emits batches; every operator works on batches in parallel |
| `"in-memory"` | each node computes its whole result before the next node starts |
| `"gpu"` | NVIDIA GPUs via `cudf-polars` |

: Engines in Polars 2.0 {.striped}

If the chosen engine can't run part of a query, Polars falls back to the
in-memory engine for it. `explain()` prints the logical plan, which is the
same for every engine. To see the streaming engine's physical plan, use
`lf.show_graph(plan_stage="physical", raw_output=True)`: it returns Graphviz
DOT text whose legend marks in-memory fallback nodes.

Streaming means a filter or `with_columns` never holds more than a few
batches at a time. Only operators that must see everything keep state:
`group_by` keeps one accumulator per group, a join keeps a hash table of one
side, a sort keeps all rows. Memory then scales with that state, not with
the input, which is how a query can run on files larger than RAM. You can
watch the batches directly:

```{python}
batches = flights_lf.select("carrier", "dep_delay").collect_batches(chunk_size=100_000)
[batch.height for batch in batches]
```

#### Row order is not guaranteed {#sec-lazy-order}

The price of parallel batches: operators that combine rows emit them in
whatever order the threads finish. The same left join, run four ways:

```{python}
keys_df = flights_df.select("carrier", "flight")
named_lf = keys_df.lazy().join(airlines_df.lazy(), on="carrier", how="left")
named_ordered_lf = keys_df.lazy().join(
    airlines_df.lazy(), on="carrier", how="left", maintain_order="left"
)
{   # does the result keep flights' row order?
    "eager DataFrame.join()": keys_df.join(airlines_df, on="carrier", how="left")
    .select(keys_df.columns).equals(keys_df),
    "collect(engine='in-memory')": named_lf.collect(engine="in-memory")
    .select(keys_df.columns).equals(keys_df),
    "collect()  (streaming)": named_lf.collect().select(keys_df.columns).equals(keys_df),
    "maintain_order='left'": named_ordered_lf.collect().select(keys_df.columns).equals(keys_df),
}
```

`maintain_order="none"` is the join default for both engines; the in-memory
engine just happens to keep the left order. Code that relied on that accident
breaks when it moves from eager to lazy. dplyr's `left_join()` keeps `x`'s
row order. (duckplyr's documentation gives the same warning about DuckDB:
results are not ordered.)

| Operation | Order under streaming | Ask for order with |
|---|---|---|
| `filter`, `select`, `with_columns`, `sort` | preserved | |
| `join` | none by default | `maintain_order="left"` (or `"right"`, `"left_right"`, …) |
| `group_by().agg()` | none, in either engine | `group_by(..., maintain_order=True)` or `.sort()` |
| `unique()` | none, in either engine | `unique(maintain_order=True)` |
| `unpivot()` | reordered under streaming | `.sort()` afterwards; there is no parameter |
| `sink_*()` | preserved by default | `maintain_order=False` is slightly faster |

: Who keeps row order {.striped}

#### Other ways to run a plan

| Call | Returns | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `lf.collect()` | `DataFrame` | |
| `lf.collect(background=True)` | `InProcessQuery`: `.fetch()` (None until done), `.fetch_blocking()`, `.cancel()` | unstable |
| `await lf.collect_async()` | `DataFrame` | for asyncio code |
| `lf.collect_batches(chunk_size=)` | an iterator of `DataFrame`s | unstable; slower than a sink |
| `pl.collect_all([lf1, lf2])` | a list of `DataFrame`s | shares common subplans (@sec-lazy-recipes) |
| `lf.sink_parquet()`, `sink_csv()`, `sink_ndjson()`, `sink_ipc()` | `None`; writes files | `lazy=True` returns a plan for `collect_all` |
| `lf.cache()` | a `LazyFrame` with a `CACHE` node | the docs say the optimizer usually does better |

: Running a plan {.striped}

### A measured example {#sec-lazy-measured}

A synthetic radiology worklist: 5 million exams over five years, with a
fixed seed, written as Parquet partitioned by year (one directory per
year, the *hive* layout `year=2025/`).

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(2025)
n_exams = 5_000_000

exams_df_raw = pl.DataFrame({
    "exam_id": np.arange(n_exams),
    "exam_date": np.datetime64("2021-01-01")
    + rng.integers(0, 5 * 365, n_exams).astype("timedelta64[D]"),
    "site": rng.choice(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"], n_exams),
    "modality": rng.choice(
        ["XR", "CT", "US", "MR", "MG", "NM"], n_exams, p=[0.45, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1, 0.07, 0.03]
    ),
    "priority": rng.choice(["routine", "urgent", "stat"], n_exams, p=[0.7, 0.2, 0.1]),
    "patient_age": rng.integers(0, 96, n_exams),
    "n_images": rng.integers(1, 2000, n_exams),
    "tat_min": rng.lognormal(4, 1, n_exams).round(1),   # report turnaround, minutes
}).with_columns(
    accession=pl.format("ACC{}", pl.col("exam_id").cast(pl.String).str.zfill(9)),
    year=pl.col("exam_date").dt.year(),
)

exams_dir = data_dir / "exams"
exams_df_raw.write_parquet(exams_dir, partition_by="year")
del exams_df_raw

sorted(str(p.relative_to(data_dir)) for p in exams_dir.rglob("*.parquet"))
```

The question: median turnaround of 2025 stat exams, by modality.

```{python}
exams_lf = pl.scan_parquet(exams_dir)   # a directory: hive partitions detected

stat_tat_lf = (
    exams_lf
    .filter(pl.col("year") == 2025, pl.col("priority") == "stat")
    .group_by("modality")
    .agg(n=pl.len(), tat_median=pl.col("tat_min").median())
    .sort("modality")
)
show_plan(stat_tat_lf)
```

The scan lists **one file**: the four other years were pruned from the
directory names alone (`year` comes from the path, so no file had to be
opened to rule it out). Within that file, 4 of 10 columns are read. The
eager version has no such option:

```{python}
def stat_tat_eager() -> pl.DataFrame:
    exams_df = pl.read_parquet(exams_dir)               # all 5 files, all 10 columns
    return (
        exams_df
        .filter(pl.col("year") == 2025, pl.col("priority") == "stat")
        .group_by("modality")
        .agg(n=pl.len(), tat_median=pl.col("tat_min").median())
        .sort("modality")
    )


assert_frame_equal(stat_tat_eager(), stat_tat_lf.collect())   # same answer
stat_tat_lf.collect()
```

Now the timing, best of three runs each. **The numbers depend on the machine
and change between renders**; the ratios are what to look at.

```{python}
def best_ms(f, runs: int = 3) -> float:
    times = []
    for _ in range(runs):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        f()
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
    return round(min(times) * 1000, 1)


timings = {
    "eager: read all, then filter": best_ms(stat_tat_eager),
    "read_parquet() alone": best_ms(lambda: pl.read_parquet(exams_dir)),
    "lazy: collect()": best_ms(stat_tat_lf.collect),
    "lazy: in-memory engine": best_ms(lambda: stat_tat_lf.collect(engine="in-memory")),
}
pl.DataFrame({"approach": list(timings), "ms": list(timings.values())}).with_columns(
    vs_eager=(pl.col("ms").first() / pl.col("ms")).round(1)
)
```

On this machine the lazy query is more than ten times faster, and both
engines are about equal: the win comes from the plan, not the engine. The
eager pipeline spends roughly half its time just reading, and it holds this
much in memory before the filter removes 98% of it:

```{python}
f"{pl.read_parquet(exams_dir).estimated_size('mb'):.0f} MB"
```

The lazy query reads one fifth of the rows and two fifths of the columns,
so it never builds that frame.

### Eager vs lazy {#sec-lazy-when}

Most eager verbs are already lazy queries of one step. In the 2.0 source,
`DataFrame.filter()` is literally
`self.lazy().filter(...)._collect_eager(...)`, and `join()`,
`with_columns()` and the rest follow the same pattern: collected at once on
the in-memory engine with the cross-step optimizations off (that is why the
eager join above kept its order). So the choice is not between two engines
but between letting the optimizer see one step or the whole query.

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| exploring a frame that fits in memory, step by step | eager |
| anything that starts from a file | `pl.scan_*()` … `.collect()` |
| a pipeline of several steps, even on an in-memory frame | `df.lazy()` … `.collect()` (CSE, sort removal, top-k still apply) |
| results that should go to disk | `sink_*()` instead of `collect()` + `write_*()` |
| several outputs from the same input | `pl.collect_all()` |

: Choosing {.striped}

**Don't collect in the middle.** A `collect()` ends the plan: whatever comes
after it can't be pushed back into the read.

```{python}
show_plan(flights_lf.collect().lazy().filter(pl.col("origin") == "JFK").select("carrier"))
```

The filter now runs over an in-memory `DF` holding all 19 columns that were
already read; compare the `SELECTION` inside the scan in @sec-lazy-explain.

**Methods that exist on only one side** (from comparing `dir()` in 2.0):

- *Eager only:* `height`, `shape`, `item()`, `rows()`, `glimpse()`,
  `sample()`, `transpose()`, `to_dummies()`, `partition_by()`, `upsample()`,
  `is_duplicated()`, `write_*()`. They need the data or its size; collect
  first.
- *Lazy only:* `explain()`, `collect*()`, `sink_*()`, `cache()`,
  `inspect()`, `pipe_with_schema()`, `show_graph()`.
- *Different signature:* `pivot()` exists on both, but a `LazyFrame` must
  know its output columns before it reads any data, and a pivot's columns
  are data values. So lazily `on_columns=` is required:

```{python}
#| error: true
flights_df.lazy().pivot("origin", index="carrier", values="dep_delay")
```

```{python}
(
    flights_df.lazy()
    .pivot("origin", on_columns=["EWR", "JFK", "LGA"], index="carrier",
           values="dep_delay", aggregate_function="len")
    .sort("carrier")
    .head(3)
    .collect()
)
```

dbplyr hits the same wall: its docs say `pivot_wider()` "cannot be lazy
because we need to look at the data to figure out what the new column names
will be", and its escape hatch, a pre-built spec, plays the role of
`on_columns=`. [Reshaping](../transform/reshape.qmd) covers `pivot()`
itself.

## Where it bites {#sec-lazy-gotchas}

| Expectation from eager code or R | Lazy Polars behaviour |
|---|---|
| a pipeline returns data | it returns a `LazyFrame`; forget `collect()` and you hold a plan |
| a typo fails on the line that has it | schema errors appear at `collect_schema()` / `explain()` / `collect()` |
| a bad value fails on the line that has it | data errors appear only at `collect()`, and only if the step runs |
| `left_join()` keeps the left row order | streaming joins don't, unless `maintain_order=` (@sec-lazy-order) |
| eager and lazy results are identical | float aggregates can differ in the last bits; compare with `assert_frame_equal` |
| a Python function is just another step | UDFs block some pushdowns |
| `collect(streaming=True)`, `collect(predicate_pushdown=False)` from older tutorials | `ArgumentRemovedError` in 2.0: use `engine="streaming"`, `optimizations=pl.QueryOptFlags(...)` |
| `lf.profile()` from older tutorials | removed in 2.0 |
| `lf.describe()` is cheap metadata | it runs the whole plan and returns a `DataFrame` |
| `lf.columns`, `lf.schema` | work, but warn (`PerformanceWarning`): use `lf.collect_schema()` |

: The differences at a glance {.striped}

### Forgetting `collect()`

A `LazyFrame` has no rows to index:

```{python}
#| error: true
jfk_late_lf["carrier"]
```

`len(lf)`, `lf.height` and `lf.write_parquet()` fail the same way. The
fix is always the same: add `.collect()` (or use `sink_parquet()`).

### Errors arrive late {#sec-lazy-errors}

Building a plan checks nothing. A typo passes silently until something
resolves the schema:

```{python}
#| error: true
typo_lf = flights_df.lazy().select("carier")   # no error here …
typo_lf.collect_schema()                        # … only here
```

`collect_schema()` resolves names and dtypes without reading data, so it
catches typos and type mismatches cheaply. It can't catch errors that depend
on the values:

```{python}
cast_lf = flights_df.lazy().with_columns(carrier_code=pl.col("carrier").cast(pl.Int64))
cast_lf.collect_schema()["carrier_code"]   # the plan type-checks
```

```{python}
#| error: true
cast_lf.collect()
```

The count in the message covers only the batch that failed, not the whole
column; the in-memory engine reports all 336,776 rows. And a broken step
whose output nobody uses never runs at all, because projection pushdown
removes it:

```{python}
cast_lf.select("year").head(1).collect()
```

### Python UDFs block pushdown

`map_elements()` runs a Python function per value; `map_batches()` runs one
on a whole Series. The optimizer can't see inside either, and treats them
differently:

```{python}
delay_hr_elements = pl.col("dep_delay").map_elements(
    lambda m: round(m / 60, 1), return_dtype=pl.Float64
)
delay_hr_batches = pl.col("dep_delay").map_batches(
    lambda s: (s / 60).round(1), return_dtype=pl.Float64
)
for udf in [delay_hr_elements, delay_hr_batches]:
    show_plan(
        flights_lf.with_columns(delay_hr=udf)
        .filter(pl.col("origin") == "JFK")
        .select("delay_hr")
    )
    print("---")
```

With `map_elements()` (element-wise, so filtering first changes nothing),
the filter still reaches the scan. With `map_batches()` the function might
depend on the whole batch, so the filter has to wait above it: the UDF runs
on all 336,776 rows instead of the 111,279 JFK flights. `LazyFrame.map_batches()`
is stronger still: it becomes an `OPAQUE_PYTHON` node that blocks both
pushdowns unless you pass `predicate_pushdown=True` /
`projection_pushdown=True`, and it assumes the schema is unchanged unless
you pass `schema=`. Native expressions avoid all of this.

## Recipes {#sec-lazy-recipes}

**Inspect a big file cheaply.** The schema and a few rows, without loading
the data (`exams_lf.select(pl.len()).collect().item()` adds the row count):

```{python}
exams_lf.collect_schema()
```

```{python}
exams_lf.head(3).collect()
```

For CSV, `collect_schema()` infers dtypes from the first
`infer_schema_length` rows (100 by default), so it is cheap but can guess
wrong.

**Filter a partitioned dataset by partition.** Any filter on the hive key
prunes directories, including ranges:

```{python}
show_plan(exams_lf.filter(pl.col("year") >= 2024).select(pl.len()))
```

**Write results without materializing them** (≈ `arrow::write_dataset(partitioning = "origin")`).
`sink_parquet()` streams batches to disk; with `pl.PartitionBy` it writes
the hive layout itself:

```{python}
(
    flights_lf
    .filter(pl.col("dep_delay") > 0)
    .sink_parquet(pl.PartitionBy(data_dir / "late_by_origin", key="origin"), mkdir=True)
)
sorted(str(p.relative_to(data_dir)) for p in (data_dir / "late_by_origin").rglob("*.parquet"))
```

The result never exists as a `DataFrame` in Python. `PartitionBy` is marked
unstable.

**Compute two summaries in one pass.** Two queries that share a scan and a
filter, collected together:

```{python}
jfk_by_carrier_lf = jfk_flights_lf.group_by("carrier").agg(n=pl.len())
jfk_by_dest_lf = jfk_flights_lf.group_by("dest").agg(avg_delay=pl.col("dep_delay").mean())

show_plan(pl.explain_all([jfk_by_carrier_lf, jfk_by_dest_lf]))

jfk_by_carrier_df, jfk_by_dest_df = pl.collect_all([jfk_by_carrier_lf, jfk_by_dest_lf])
jfk_by_carrier_df.shape, jfk_by_dest_df.shape
```

`pl.explain_all()` shows the shared `CACHE`: the file is scanned and filtered
once. Two separate `collect()` calls would do both twice.

```{python}
#| include: false
tmp.cleanup()
```
